links.note: In 1102 the man says that medicines for other ailments are things other than the ailment (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). In 1241 the woman, apart from him, asks her heart to think of any medicine at all (எனைத்தொன்றும் ... மருந்து) for her sickness. Read together, 1102 explains why her heart has nothing to offer: the only cure is the absent person who caused the illness.

1195 asks what those we love can do for us if they do not love in return (தாம் காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1242 draws the conclusion and turns it on her own heart: since he has no love (காதல் அவரிலர் ஆக), its suffering is folly (நோவது பேதைமை). The first states the uselessness of one-sided love, the second names persisting in it as foolishness.

1308, which Parimelazhagar gives to the man during a sulk, asks what use suffering is where there is no lover who recognises that one suffers (நோதல் எவன் ... அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 1242 has the woman tell her heart that suffering is folly when he has no love (நோவது பேதைமை). Both speakers, from either side of the relationship, make pain depend for its point on the other's loving awareness of it.

1243 asks the heart why it sits and suffers in thought (இருந்துள்ளி என் பரிதல்) when he has no pitying thought. 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்) her heart is there only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய). Both describe sitting and remembering as self-inflicted harm, and each blames the heart for it.

1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர் நெஞ்சத்து). 1243 gives her own bleak answer: a compassionate thought of her does not exist in the one who caused the sickness (பரிந்துள்ளல் பைதல்நோய் செய்தார்கண் இல்). The question of 1204 has by chapter 125 become a settled premise for scolding her heart.

1170 says that if her eyes could travel to where he is as her heart does (உள்ளம் போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in tears. 1244 turns the same contrast into a request: heart, take the eyes with you when you go (கண்ணும் கொளச் சேறி), because left behind they consume her with wanting to see him. Both rest on the idea that the heart can reach him by thought and the eyes cannot.

In 1244 the eyes eat her (இவை என்னைத் தின்னும்) in their longing to see him; in 1296 it is the heart that stays in order to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய இருந்தது என் நெஞ்சு). The same verb of being devoured is applied to two of her own faculties, so that between the two verses neither eyes nor heart is on her side.

1283 says that though he disregards her and does only as he pleases, her eyes will not rest without seeing him (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்). 1244 says the eyes, wanting to see him (அவர்க் காணல் உற்று), eat her. Both make the eyes an appetite of their own that her judgment of him does not govern.

1245 asks the heart whether one can abandon as an enemy (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not respond when she draws close (யாம் உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்). 1292 complains that the heart, even having seen that he is not close (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்), goes to him on the thought that he will not be hostile (செறாஅர் என). The two share the pair உறாதவர் / செறு, and show the same refusal to treat coldness as enmity, once owned by her and once blamed on the heart.

807, on old friendship, says that those whose bond came by the way of love do not cut off love even when ruinous things are done to them (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). 1245 asks whether she can let him go as an enemy merely because he does not return her closeness. The logic of long friendship in the Book of Wealth, that injury does not license abandonment, reappears as a lover's rhetorical question.

1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot even sulk and then be reconciled (புலந்துணராய்), so its present anger is a false heat (பொய்க்காய்வு காய்தி). 1294 makes the same charge: the heart will not first raise a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), so no one will plan with it. In both the heart is accused of being incapable of the sulk it pretends to.

1286 says that when she sees him she sees no faults, and when she does not see him she sees nothing but faults (காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). 1246 calls the heart's anger in his absence false because it never survives the sight of him (காதலர்க் கண்டால் புலந்துணராய்). 1286 states the pattern plainly; 1246 uses it to discredit the anger felt while apart.

1163 pictures desire and shame hanging from the two ends of a carrying pole that is her life, in a body that cannot bear them (காமமும் நாணும் உயிர் காவாத் தூங்கும் என் நோனா உடம்பின்). 1247 states the same double load without the image and asks her heart to drop one of them, since she cannot bear both (யானோ பொறேன் இவ்விரண்டு). The earlier verse describes the balance; this one asks for it to end.

1247 leaves open which of desire and shame is to go (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). 1251, opening the next chapter, reports the outcome: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint that shame had bolted (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் ... நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). The choice she offers her heart in 1247 is settled in 1251 by force, not by decision.

1248 calls the heart a fool for going after the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்) while grieving that he gives no grace. 1293 asks the heart whether it follows him as it likes (பெட்டாங்கு அவர் பின் செலல்) because the ruined have no friends. Both speak of the heart 'going behind him' as a desertion of her that she can see but not stop.

967, on honour, says that being called ruined is better than living by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின் சென்று ஒருவன் வாழ்தலின்); Parimelazhagar takes this of following scorners for gain. 1248 calls her heart a fool for going behind the one who left without grace (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய் பேதை). The standard of honour from the Book of Wealth is the one she applies to her own heart, though in love she cannot enforce it.

1128 says that because her lover is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவராக) she fears to eat anything hot lest he be scalded. 1249 uses almost the same clause (உள்ளத்தார் காதலவராக) to ask the heart whom it goes out to look for. The conceit that was playful tenderness during union becomes, in separation, an argument against the heart's wandering.

1130 says he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்) while the town says he lives apart and is a stranger. 1249 asks her heart to whom it is going when he is inside it. In 1130 the town fails to know where he really dwells; in 1249 her own heart is the one that acts as if it did not know.

In 1250 she says that if she keeps in her heart the man who left without coming close (துறந்தாரை நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா), she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்); Parimelazhagar frames this as a case for forgetting him. In 1262 she tells her friend that if she forgets him today, beauty will leave her and the bangles slip from her arms (இன்று மறப்பின் ... கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). The two speeches give opposite accounts of whether remembering or forgetting costs her beauty; both are a speaker's words in the moment, and the conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's reading of the settings.

1207 says she does not know how to forget, and that even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1250 says that holding him in her heart will cost her yet more beauty. Both count remembering him as a harm to herself, while 1207 adds that forgetting is not available to her.

71 asks whether there is any bolt that can shut love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the tears of the loving proclaim it. 1251 uses the same word தாழ்: shame is the bolt on the door of restraint, and the axe of desire breaks the door (நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). In the Book of Virtue affection cannot be bolted in and that is to its credit; in the Book of Love the bolt exists and its breaking is told as her defeat.

In 1134 the man says the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும் நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). In 1251 the woman says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted by shame. The two verses are built alike, with desire as a force and shame as the device that fails against it, once for the man and once for the woman.

57 says that guarding women by confinement achieves nothing and the guard their own நிறை keeps is the best (மகளிர் நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை). 1251 has a woman say that this very நிறை, pictured as a door bolted by shame, is broken by desire for her husband. The dramatised speech shows the inner guard of 57 at its limit, though here what breaks it is love for her own partner and not a lapse of fidelity.

1167 says she swims the flood of desire and sees no shore, and even at midnight only she is awake (யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்). 1252 says desire has no pity (கண் இன்று), for it sets her heart to work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both mark midnight, when Parimelazhagar notes all others rest, as the hour that shows desire does not release her.

In 1136 the man says his eyes cannot close because of her, so even at midnight he thinks of mounting the palmyra horse (மடலூர்தல் யாமத்தும் உள்ளுவேன்). In 1252 the woman says desire rules and works her heart even at midnight. The sleepless midnight belongs to both sexes: for him it produces a plan for public display, for her an inward servitude.

1161 and 1253 open with the same words, 'I would hide it' (மறைப்பேன்மன் யான்). In 1161 the sickness rises like spring water the more one bales it (இறைப்பவர்க்கு ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்); in 1253 desire shows itself like a sneeze without her intending it (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல் போல் தோன்றிவிடும்). One image gives the pressure that grows under concealment, the other the sudden involuntary release.

1253 likens desire to a sneeze that appears without one's intending it; Parimelazhagar glosses that it cannot be held in. In 1318 the man does stifle a sneeze (தும்முச் செறுப்ப), and she weeps that he is hiding from her that his people are thinking of him. The sneeze is in both an involuntary sign of what is within, and 1318 shows that even suppressing it is read as a disclosure.

1138 says desire does not consider that they are firm in restraint or deserve pity, but passes beyond secrecy and comes out in public (காமம் மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்). 1254 ends with the same words (என் காமம் மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்) after her admission that she used to call herself one who had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்). The general statement in 1138 becomes in 1254 her own experience of being proved wrong about herself.

1180 says it is not hard for the town to get the secret of those like her, whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). 1254 says her desire goes past concealment into the public place (மன்று படும்). 1180 supplies a means by which the exposure described in 1254 happens: her own eyes announce it.

966, on honour, asks what is gained by going and standing behind those who scorn one (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை), since it brings neither fame nor heaven. 1255 says the dignity of not going after those who have turned hostile (செற்றார் பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the lovesick do not know. 1255 names the standard of the honour chapter as a real greatness and then places the lover outside its reach; Parimelazhagar takes 'going after' here as unbroken thinking of him.

1245 asks whether she can abandon as hostile (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not answer her love. 1255 turns that private question into a general statement: not following the hostile (செற்றார் பின் செல்லா) is a dignity unknown to those with love's sickness (காமநோய் உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று). The word செற்றார் links them, and the second explains why the first could only be a rhetorical question.

1255 states in general terms that the lovesick do not know the dignity of not going after one who is hostile. 1256 applies it to herself with irony: how gracious (அளித்தரோ) is this grief, which wants her to go after the one who is hostile (செற்றவர் பின் சேறல் வேண்டி). The pair moves from a maxim about lovers to her own case, and Parimelazhagar reads அளித்து as mockery.

In 1168 she calls the night அளித்து, pitiable or kindly, because having put every living thing to sleep it has no companion but her. In 1256 she uses the same word of her grief (அளித்தரோ ... துயர்), which Parimelazhagar takes as scorn. In both she speaks to her tormentor in the language of grace and pity, which is how these monologues voice bitterness.

1297 says that, caught up with a foolish heart that cannot forget him, she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்). 1257 says she knows nothing of a thing called shame (நாண் என ஒன்றோ அறியலம்) when the one she cherishes does out of desire what she longs for. The two verses give the same loss of shame from two moments, separation in 1297 and reunion in 1257.

In 1247 she cannot bear desire and shame together and asks her heart to give up one (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). In 1257 the matter is settled in his presence: when he does what she longs for, shame is simply not known to her. The conflict that is unbearable in his absence does not arise once he is there.

1258 asks whether the humble speech of that thief of many deceptions is not the weapon that breaks their womanhood (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை), which Parimelazhagar glosses as her restraint. 1324 says that within the sulk itself arises the weapon that breaks 'my' heart (உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை); Parimelazhagar gives it to the woman. The shared phrase உடைக்கும் படை frames her resolve as a fortification, attacked from outside by his words in 1258 and from inside the quarrel in 1324.

985 says that bowing is the strength of those who accomplish things and the weapon by which the worthy turn their opponents (பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 1258 calls her lover's lowly speech (பணிமொழி) the weapon that breaks her firmness. Humility as a படை is praised in the ethics of the worthy, and in the love poems the woman sees the same device used on her and calls its user a thief.

555 asks whether the tears of those who suffer under a ruler are not the weapon that wears away his wealth (கண்ணீர் அன்றே செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). 1258 has the same form of question: are his humble words not the weapon that breaks our womanhood (பணிமொழி அன்றோ ... உடைக்கும் படை). In both a soft thing, tears or gentle speech, is named as the real weapon against something that looks strong.

1284 tells her friend that she went intending to sulk, but her heart forgot that and went to unite (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன் ... கூடற்கண் சென்றது என் நெஞ்சு). 1259 tells the same event with one more step: she went away meaning to sulk (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன்) and embraced him on seeing her heart begin to join him (நெஞ்சம் கலத்தல் உறுவது கண்டு). In 1284 the heart acts alone; in 1259 she watches it and gives in.

1290 gives the man's account: she sulked with her eyes only and then, more eager than he for the embrace, lost her composure (புல்லுதல் என்னினும் தான் விதுப்புற்று). 1259 gives hers: she set out to sulk and embraced him (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன் புல்லினேன்). The two verses report the collapse of a sulk from each side and agree on what happened.

1267, spoken while he is still away, asks whether on his return she will sulk, embrace, or do both (புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்). 1259 is the answer after the fact: she intended the first and did the second (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன் புல்லினேன்). The same two verbs carry the plan in one verse and its failure in the other.

1287 asks what use it is to sulk when one knows the sulk will prove false (பொய்த்தல் அறிந்து என் புலந்து), like those who jump into a stream knowing it will carry them off. 1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்) can ever say they will hold out in a sulk. One image is of being swept away and the other of melting, and both conclude that the sulk cannot be sustained.

1259 narrates one occasion: she went away to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him. 1260 turns it into a general question about people whose hearts melt like fat in fire, and whether 'we will stand in a sulk' (ஊடி நிற்பேம் எனல்) is even open to them. The second verse gives the reason for the first.
